events.description: A visible explosion occurs on the port side of HMS Barham, ejecting a plume of smoke and debris upward and outward; this is the first clear detonation following the title card.
A second, larger explosion erupts from the midships area of HMS Barham, producing a massive column of dark smoke and visibly distorting the ship's structure.
A third major explosion occurs near the stern or aft superstructure, causing further structural collapse and a sharp increase in smoke volume; the ship begins listing heavily.
A fourth explosion is visible amidships or forward, coinciding with rapid capsizing; smoke continues to billow as the hull tilts sharply to starboard.

A small, bright flash appears above the water near the stern of the sinking ship in frame f7 (7.5s), consistent with a secondary explosion or ammunition cook-off; it is visible as a brief white speck against the sky and disappears by f8 (8.0s).
A large, violent explosion erupts from the burning vessel, producing a massive plume of water, smoke, and debris that expands outward rapidly.

A massive, sustained underwater or surface explosion on a ship, producing a large fireball, violent ejection of debris and water, followed by rapidly expanding dark smoke plumes that obscure the vessel over time.

A massive, sustained explosion or detonation occurs on or near the water surface, producing an enormous, rapidly expanding column of dark smoke and debris that rises and billows upward over several seconds. The initial blast (f0–f4) shows violent ejection of material; subsequent frames (f5–f15) show the smoke plume ascending and dispersing, with no visible fireball but clear evidence of a powerful energetic release consistent with a large-scale explosion (e.g., naval ordnance test or ship detonation).

A large, sustained plume of dense smoke rises from a surface (likely water), indicating a major explosion or fire event. The smoke column expands and billows continuously across all frames, with visible turbulence and rising motion consistent with a powerful detonation or catastrophic fire.

A large, sustained column of dark smoke rises from the sea surface, expanding and billowing upward over time, consistent with a massive underwater or surface explosion (e.g., naval ordnance test or ship detonation). No fireball is visible, but the rapid vertical development and volume of smoke indicate a powerful blast event.

A large, sustained column of smoke and debris rises from the ocean surface, consistent with a massive underwater or surface explosion (e.g., nuclear test or large ordnance detonation). The plume expands vertically and horizontally over time, with visible turbulent motion and possible condensation effects at the base. No fireball is visible in these frames, but the scale and dynamics strongly indicate an explosive origin rather than natural phenomena like a waterspout.

A large, rising column of dark smoke and debris erupts from the ocean surface, expanding upward and outward over several seconds—consistent with a massive underwater or surface explosion (e.g., nuclear test or large ordnance detonation). The plume grows in volume and height, with turbulent cloud dynamics indicating rapid energy release.
